title: Sitharaman: RBI Will Keep Fighting Rupee Volatility, But Will Not 'Fix' the Currency's Level
excerpt: Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, the Finance Minister blamed the rupee's 'very significant' slide over 18 months on external factors, noted it recovered 1% on Monday after the RBI's weekend measures — and called the debate on LTCG and STT rationalisation 'healthy' ahead of the February 1 Budget.
body:
• Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said Tuesday the RBI will continue efforts to prevent excessive rupee volatility, but is not trying to "fix" the currency at a level — it should find its own.
  • The rupee appreciated about 1% on Monday after the RBI's weekend measures, and strengthened further to ₹94.96 in early trade on Tuesday.
  • The RBI's weekend package created a special window for oil marketing companies to take dollar demand off the spot market, and tightened rules on forex derivatives to curb speculative bets against the rupee.
  • On taxes, Sitharaman called the debate over rationalising long-term capital gains tax and the securities transaction tax "healthy," said she will hear it "keenly" — and noted Budget preparation for 2027-28, likely presented February 1, has begun.

India's Finance Minister used a Bloomberg stage on Tuesday to deliver two messages at once: the central bank will keep leaning against the rupee's slide, and investors lobbying for capital-gains tax relief will have to wait for the Budget. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026, Nirmala Sitharaman said the rupee has depreciated "very significantly" over the past year and a half mainly because of global uncertainties, even as India's macroeconomic fundamentals — including foreign exchange reserves — remain strong, The Hindu reported.

"I am sure there are efforts which the RBI would take further to make sure that rupee doesn't become too volatile."

— Nirmala Sitharaman, Finance Minister

Defending the currency without defending a number

The distinction she drew is the one currency traders listen for. The RBI's measures, she said, aim to prevent volatility, not to fix the rupee's level: "We would appreciate it if the rupee finds its own (level)." The immediate backdrop is the package the RBI announced over the weekend — a special window for oil marketing companies that moves their dollar demand away from the spot market, and tighter rules on forex derivatives trades aimed at speculative positioning against the rupee. Those measures, she noted, supported the currency as it appreciated 1% on Monday, and it strengthened again to ₹94.96 in early trade on Tuesday.

The longer defence has been built in layers since June, when the government and RBI moved to attract dollars during the West Asia crisis: expanding the Fully Accessible Route list for foreign investors in government securities, tax exemptions on FPI interest and capital gains from G-Secs, and an RBI swap facility for FCNR(B) deposits of three to five years. Banks mobilised $133 billion under that FCNR(B) scheme by its August 31 close — a figure that underlines how central diaspora deposits have become to the currency strategy, and why the closing date was advanced by a month on the strength of the response.

The tax question she would not answer

Asked about rationalisation of taxes in the securities market, Sitharaman said the debate around the securities transaction tax and long-term capital gains tax is "healthy" and that she will "keenly" hear it — then closed the door on specifics. "We are very close to the Budget, and the preparation for the Budget has started. It may not be the best time for me to say what I will or what I will not consider," she said. The Union Budget 2027-28 is likely to be presented on February 1. Her remarks nonetheless landed on a market primed for them: the LTCG comment was one of the factors credited in Tuesday's sharp equity rebound. Private capital, she added, is flowing into renewables, semiconductors and chip design, biosimilars, pharmaceuticals and aircraft maintenance — the sectors New Delhi is counting on to keep the investment side of the external account as strong as the deposit side.
